_readme: Reference content (static, not fetched live) for every climate oscillation the site tracks: what each one physically is, which ski regions it actually affects and in which direction, how often it updates, and — critically — how far ahead it is genuinely predictive rather than just describing what already happened. The _primer block is the conceptual background: what climate oscillations are as a family, and why the ocean-driven ones are forecastable months ahead while the atmosphere-driven ones are not.

_primer.title: What climate oscillations are, and why some are forecastable
paragraphs: ENSO — El Niño and La Niña — is the famous one, but it is a single member of a family. A climate oscillation is a large-scale pattern in the ocean or atmosphere that keeps flipping between a small number of preferred states, on timescales from a few weeks to several decades. Each one shifts where the jet stream sits, and therefore where storms go.

The most useful thing to understand about them for trip planning: they mostly redistribute snow rather than create or destroy it. A phase that starves the Pacific Northwest is often the same phase feeding California and the southern Rockies. That is why this site ranks regions against each other instead of forecasting a single global 'good' or 'bad' winter — in almost every phase, somewhere is winning.

The mechanism is indirect but well established. An unusually warm or cool patch of ocean changes where tropical thunderstorm activity clusters. That shift in convection launches large atmospheric waves (Rossby waves) that propagate out of the tropics and into the mid-latitudes, where they reposition the ridges and troughs that steer storms. That is how a sea-surface temperature anomaly on the equator ends up deciding whether it snows in Colorado.
Which brings up the single most important distinction on this page — what is actually oscillating, because it determines how far ahead the signal is worth anything:

families.label: Ocean-driven — slow, and genuinely forecastable
families.text: Water has enormous heat capacity. Once a large patch of ocean is anomalously warm or cool, it stays that way for months or years — the ocean remembers. That thermal memory is what makes these signals predictable at seasonal range, and it is why ENSO can meaningfully inform a booking decision several months out.

families.label: Atmosphere-driven — fast, and largely chaotic
families.text: Air has almost no thermal memory. These patterns are the atmosphere reorganizing itself, and they can flip from one extreme to the other within a few weeks. Deterministic skill runs out after roughly 1–2 weeks, and seasonal prediction of them remains an unsolved research problem. Read them as a description of the pattern you are currently in — excellent for explaining why a season is running hot or cold, close to useless for booking a year ahead.

_primer.closing: These patterns also interfere with each other, constructively and destructively. A negative NAO can override what ENSO 'should' be doing in the Northeast for weeks at a time; a cool PDO can blunt an El Niño's effect on the West Coast. That is why this site assigns each region a single primary driver — whichever one the research says actually dominates there — rather than averaging every index into one mushy number.

timescale_ladder.note: Not tracked here — too short-fused for trip planning, but it is what makes a given fortnight stormy.
Atmospheric. Describes the pattern you are in now.
Ocean. Peaks in austral spring; matters most to Australia.
Ocean-atmosphere coupled. The workhorse seasonal signal.
Ocean. A background state, not a forecast.

oni.name: ONI — Oceanic Niño Index (ENSO)
oni.what_it_is: Sea-surface temperature in the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, measured as an anomaly against the long-term average. It is coupled to the atmosphere above it: warm water shifts tropical convection east, which weakens the trade winds, which keeps the water warm — a feedback loop that locks a phase in for the better part of a year.
oni.timescale: Phases last 9–12+ months; the cycle recurs every 2–7 years
oni.positive_effect: Strengthens the subtropical jet and pushes it south. Wetter for California, the Southwest and the southern Rockies; drier for the Pacific Northwest, the Northern Rockies and BC. Suppresses Arctic outbreaks into the Northeast. Strongly favors the central Andes. Warm and dry for Australia.
oni.negative_effect: Essentially the mirror image. The storm track locks onto the Pacific Northwest, Northern Rockies and BC interior; California and the Southwest dry out (the classic 'Southwest drought' pattern); the central Andes turn dry; Australia turns cooler and wetter.
oni.regions_affected: Nearly all of them — this is the only signal with genuine global reach. Weakest over the European Alps and only loosely coupled to Japan.
oni.latency: NOAA CPC publishes each update ~2 weeks after the month ends. Each value is itself a 3-month running average of equatorial Pacific sea-surface temperature anomalies (e.g. "MJJ" = May-June-July averaged together), so it's a smoothed, lagging read — not a same-day number.
oni.horizon_short: 3-9 months, once a phase is established
oni.horizon_detail: ENSO is the most predictable ocean-atmosphere pattern at seasonal timescales, which is why it's the primary driver of this site's regional calls. Once a phase locks in — typically by early-to-mid summer for the following winter — forecasts carry real skill 3 to 9 months out. The exception is forecasts made in Northern Hemisphere spring (roughly February-May): ENSO predictions issued during this window are historically much less reliable, a well-documented effect called the "spring predictability barrier." Read a spring ONI reading as a weaker signal than the same number would be in October.

nao.name: NAO — North Atlantic Oscillation
nao.what_it_is: A pressure seesaw between the semi-permanent low near Iceland and the high near the Azores. The pressure difference between them sets how strong and how far north the Atlantic jet stream runs.
nao.timescale: Days to weeks; can flip several times within one season
nao.positive_effect: A strong, zonal (west-to-east) Atlantic jet. Mild and wet for northern Europe, mild for the Northeast US, and a higher freezing level in the Alps — the risky pattern for anything below roughly 2,000m. Cold air stays locked up over Canada.
nao.negative_effect: A weaker, buckled jet that lets cold air push south. Raises the odds of Nor'easters tracking up the US East Coast and of cold, snowy spells reaching central Europe — the best large-scale pattern the Northeast and the lower Alps can ask for.
nao.regions_affected: Northeast US / Eastern Canada and the European Alps, where it outweighs ENSO. This site treats both regions as NAO-primary.
nao.update_frequency: Monthly (a noisier daily index also exists; this site uses the monthly value)
nao.latency: Finalizes shortly after each month ends.
nao.horizon_short: 1-4 weeks — mostly describes what already happened
nao.horizon_detail: NAO is a fast-moving, largely chaotic atmospheric pattern, not a slow ocean signal like ENSO. Deterministic skill runs out after roughly 1-2 weeks, and even the best seasonal forecast systems have only weak-to-moderate skill predicting it months in advance — seasonal NAO prediction is still an active, unsolved research problem. Treat the NAO value shown on this site as a description of the pattern that just occurred (useful for explaining why a region's season is running hot or cold), not a forecast of what's coming next.

ao.name: AO — Arctic Oscillation
ao.what_it_is: A measure of how tightly the polar vortex is holding together — essentially the strength of the ring of winds circling the Arctic. Closely related to the NAO, and often moving with it.
ao.timescale: Days to weeks; longer when a stratospheric warming event is in play
ao.positive_effect: A strong, tight polar vortex. Cold air stays bottled up near the pole, leaving the mid-latitudes milder — bad news for anywhere relying on Arctic air for cold, such as the Northeast US and lower-elevation Europe.
ao.negative_effect: A weak or displaced vortex that lets lobes of Arctic air spill south into the mid-latitudes. This is the setup behind most major cold outbreaks in the eastern US and Europe.
ao.regions_affected: Northern Hemisphere generally, most visibly the Northeast US and Europe. Tracked here as context rather than as any region's primary driver, since its effect largely overlaps with NAO.
ao.latency: Finalizes shortly after each month ends.
ao.horizon_short: 2-6 weeks, longer during a stratospheric warming event
ao.horizon_detail: Closely related to NAO and similarly hard to predict for the same chaotic-atmosphere reasons. The one exception: AO gets a real predictability boost when a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) is detected in the polar vortex — those events can presage a negative AO / cold outbreak at the surface 2-6 weeks later. Absent an active SSW signal, treat AO the same way as NAO: it's telling you what's happening now, not what's coming this winter.

pna.name: PNA — Pacific/North American Pattern
pna.what_it_is: A standing wave train arcing across the North Pacific into North America, describing where the ridges and troughs sit over the continent. It is the pattern that decides whether the West or the East gets the cold and the storms — the two are usually opposed.
pna.positive_effect: Ridge over western North America, trough over the east. Warmer and drier for the West (Sierra, PNW, Rockies); colder and stormier for the Midwest and East.
pna.negative_effect: Trough over the western US — colder and wetter for the Cascades, Sierra and Rockies, and milder, drier conditions for the East. The strongest negative PNA episode in over 50 years drove the record Christmas-week snowfall west of the Cascades in 2021.
pna.regions_affected: Western North America most directly, with the opposite sign for the East. Tends to run positive during El Niño and negative during La Niña, so it doubles as a check on whether the atmosphere is actually delivering what ENSO implies.
pna.update_frequency: Monthly (a daily index also exists; this site uses the monthly value)
pna.latency: Finalizes shortly after each month ends.
pna.horizon_short: 1-2 weeks of real skill — a pattern description, not a season forecast
pna.horizon_detail: PNA describes where the ridge and trough sit over North America, and it flips the West and East against each other: negative PNA puts a trough over the western US (colder, wetter West; milder, drier East), positive PNA ridges over the West and drives cold into the East. It is strongly related to ENSO — El Niño tends toward positive PNA, La Niña toward negative — so on this site it mostly serves as a check on whether the atmosphere is actually delivering what the current ENSO phase implies. Like NAO and AO it is a fast atmospheric pattern, so read it as a nowcast rather than a seasonal outlook.

pdo.name: PDO — Pacific Decadal Oscillation
pdo.what_it_is: A long-lived pattern of sea-surface temperature across the North Pacific, often described as an ENSO-like shape but operating on a vastly slower clock. It is a background state of the ocean rather than an event.
pdo.timescale: Months to years, sometimes holding one phase for a decade or more
pdo.positive_effect: Amplifies El Niño's usual West Coast signature — wetter California and Southwest, drier Pacific Northwest — and blunts La Niña's.
pdo.negative_effect: Amplifies La Niña's signature — wetter Pacific Northwest, drier California and Southwest — and blunts El Niño's.
pdo.regions_affected: The North American West Coast. On this site it never replaces a region's ENSO call; it scales the Sierra/California and PNW meters up or down depending on whether it currently agrees with or opposes the live ENSO phase.
pdo.latency: Finalizes shortly after each month ends.
pdo.horizon_short: Persists for months to years — a backdrop, not a forecast
pdo.horizon_detail: PDO is fundamentally different from the fast atmospheric patterns: it's a slow-moving ocean temperature pattern that typically holds its phase for months to years, sometimes over a decade. It doesn't predict any specific storm, week, or month by itself. What it does is modulate how strongly a given ENSO event actually shows up on the West Coast — a warm PDO tends to amplify El Niño's effects there, a cool PDO tends to amplify La Niña's. Read the current PDO phase as season-long context, not a forecast input on its own.

sam.name: SAM / AAO — Southern Annular Mode
sam.what_it_is: How far north or south the belt of Southern Ocean westerly winds is sitting — the Southern Hemisphere's counterpart to the AO. That belt carries the cold fronts that make the Australian and southern Andean winters.
sam.positive_effect: The westerly belt contracts poleward toward Antarctica, so cold fronts track south of the ski fields instead of over them. The classic setup for a thin, late-starting, early-finishing Australian season.
sam.negative_effect: The belt expands north onto the Australian Alps and the southern Andes, driving more frequent frontal passages and snowfall. This is the single best large-scale signal an Australian season can get.
sam.regions_affected: Australia above all — Australia's Bureau of Meteorology identifies SAM as having the strongest relationship with Australian snowfall of any climate driver, ahead of ENSO, which is why this site treats Australia as SAM-primary. Also influences the southern Andes and New Zealand.
sam.update_frequency: Monthly (NOAA CPC publishes it as the Antarctic Oscillation, AAO)
sam.latency: Finalizes shortly after each month ends.
sam.horizon_short: 1-3 weeks — but it is the strongest driver Australia has
sam.horizon_detail: SAM tracks how far north or south the Southern Ocean westerly storm belt sits. Negative SAM pushes those cold fronts north onto the Australian Alps and the southern Andes; positive SAM pulls them south toward Antarctica and away from the ski fields. Australia's Bureau of Meteorology identifies SAM as having the strongest relationship with Australian snowfall of any climate driver — stronger than ENSO — which is why this site treats the Australian region as SAM-primary rather than ENSO-primary. Its predictability is short, though, so it is far more useful for reading a season in progress than for booking a year ahead.

iod.name: IOD — Indian Ocean Dipole
iod.what_it_is: The sea-surface temperature difference between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean. That gradient controls how much moisture is available to weather systems heading toward Australia.
iod.timescale: Seasonal, typically developing mid-year and peaking in austral spring
iod.positive_effect: Cooler water off Indonesia and northwestern Australia cuts the moisture supply feeding cold fronts crossing southeastern Australia — drying out the back half of the ski season.
iod.negative_effect: Warmer water near Australia increases moisture availability, and is associated with deeper than average Australian snowpack.
iod.regions_affected: Australia, primarily, and concentrated in late winter and spring rather than across the whole season — so a positive IOD threatens a September trip more than a July one.
iod.latency: Roughly 1-2 months behind, and the feed sometimes lags further; the site shows the latest month actually published.
iod.horizon_short: Seasonal, but concentrated in late winter/spring
iod.horizon_detail: IOD measures the sea-surface temperature gradient across the tropical Indian Ocean and mainly matters for Australia. A positive IOD cuts the moisture supply feeding into cold fronts crossing southeastern Australia, drying out the back half of the season; a negative IOD is associated with deeper Australian snowpack. Unlike ENSO, its effect on snow depth is concentrated in late winter and spring rather than across the whole season, so a positive IOD is more of a threat to a September trip than a July one.
